# Route X1 — Investigative Interviewing Science

Grounding for the coaching assistant (CH-2, AST-1..10), subject-fidelity rules (PRB-4, SUB-*), the evasion taxonomy (EVL-8), rubric anchors (EVL-7), and KPI-1 plausibility. 14 Google web searches run (floor was 6). GDK and Context7 were not required for this route per task instructions and were not used.

## Q1 — Evidence-based interviewing models

**PEACE / Cognitive Interview (CI/ECI).** PEACE (Preparation and Planning, Engage and Explain, Account, Closure, Evaluate) is the UK's non-accusatorial framework; its "Account" phase draws on the Cognitive Interview — context reinstatement, report-everything, varied retrieval order, change-of-perspective. Summaries of the CI meta-analytic literature converge on roughly 25-35% more correct recalled details than standard interviews, with only a small rise in minor errors and no rise in confabulation. Confidence: high — long-replicated, multiple independent secondary summaries agree. Source: [The PEACE Model of Investigative Interviewing](https://www.slideshare.net/slideshow/the-peace-model-of-investigative-interviewing/76441687); [Bringing PEACE (Schollum)](https://www.fis-international.com/assets/Uploads/resources/Schollum-PEACE.pdf) (undated practice synthesis, not itself a primary meta-analysis — treat with care). Maps to AST-1/AST-6 (coach assesses the *question*, not just the answer) and CH-2 (favor open/probing form in suggested follow-ups).

**Strategic Use of Evidence (SUE).** Granhag & Hartwig's program: withhold evidence until the subject commits to a full, uncorroborated account, then disclose it strategically (timing — late rather than early disclosure is specifically shown to help; framing — gradual/incremental disclosure vs. all-at-once) to expose statement-evidence inconsistency, which deceptive subjects (who don't know what the interviewer holds) tend to produce more than truthful ones. One cited lab figure: SUE-trained interviewers reached 85.4% deception-detection accuracy vs. 56.1% for untrained interviewers (Swedish studies). Confidence: medium for the mechanism (timing/framing matters, replicated across several Granhag/Hartwig studies) and medium for the specific 85.4%/56.1% figures (could not verify the primary citation this session, only secondary mentions). Sources: [Strategic Use of Evidence in Investigation Interviews](https://www.caseiq.com/?p=5891); [Strategic disclosure of evidence to detect deception](https://researchportal.port.ac.uk/en/publications/strategic-disclosure-of-evidence-to-detect-deception-towards-a-ne/) (Portsmouth research portal, author page, undated abstract). Direct mapping: SCN-4/SCN-10 (scripted evidence release) and AST-3 are literally operationalizing SUE's core mechanic — the scenario engine's scripted, timed evidence release IS a SUE implementation, and the coach's "neutral follow-up using the evidence in the answer" is SUE's statement-evidence-inconsistency probe recast as a question suggestion rather than a confrontation.

**Verifiability Approach (VA).** Asks interviewees to provide checkable detail; truth-tellers volunteer more verifiable specifics because they have nothing to fear from verification, liars often give detail that sounds rich but resists checking. Found only secondary mentions alongside CBCA/RM this session, no primary effect size retrieved. Confidence: low (concept well established in the field from general knowledge, not independently re-verified by a primary source this search pass).

**Reality Monitoring (RM) and CBCA.** Both are verbal content-analysis methods applied post-hoc to a statement's transcript (not real-time question strategies). RM criteria include perceptual/contextual/affective detail; CBCA uses ~19 criteria (e.g., quantity of detail, contextual embedding, reproduction of conversation). Research says RM discriminates above chance at accuracy comparable to CBCA, and is easier to apply; meta-analyses show CBCA/RM validity "above chance" but lab paradigms often lack ecological validity. Confidence: medium — the "above chance, comparable to CBCA" claim recurs across multiple 2020s papers, but no single current meta-analytic accuracy percentage was retrieved. Source: [Optimizing CBCA and RM research (UCM)](https://docta.ucm.es/entities/publication/ec01806a-e5d9-41d9-80cd-5745323fb056/full); [Using an example statement... CBCA, RM, SCAN (Portsmouth)](https://researchportal.port.ac.uk/en/publications/using-an-example-statement-increases-information-but-does-not-inc/). Mapping: these are scoring tools for the *coach/scorer*, not interviewing prescriptions for the investigator — relevant to how the assistant or the independent scorer (SOL-5, EVL-3) might post-hoc score a transcript's content quality, not to the follow-up-question generator.

**Cognitive-load and unanticipated-question approaches (Vrij).** Three techniques: (1) impose cognitive load (e.g., reverse-order recall), (2) encourage the interviewee to say more, (3) ask unanticipated questions (spatial/temporal detail, or an unexpected format like "draw it"). Liars must invent answers on the spot, inhibit the truth, and verify their lie isn't detectable — raising cognitive load and producing more cues. One cited result: this approach reached 71% total detection accuracy vs. 56% for a standard approach (67%/67% truth/lie split vs. 57%/47%). Confidence: medium — consistent with the broader Vrij corpus, numbers plausible and specific, but drawn from a single secondary synthesis this pass, not the primary paper. Source: [Sorting the liars from the truth tellers (Portsmouth)](https://researchportal.port.ac.uk/en/publications/sorting-the-liars-from-the-truth-tellers-the-benefits-of-asking-u/). Mapping: directly actionable for AST-3/CH-2 — a "neutral follow-up" that asks for an unanticipated spatial/temporal/sequence detail (not just "what happened next") is the single most evidence-backed lever available for a text-only coach; it is also cheap to prompt-engineer (ask for order-of-events, a layout description, or timing detail tied to the evidence just disclosed).

**Asymmetric Information Management (AIM) and the Model Statement technique.** Not found via primary sources this pass — searches returned no results on these specific named techniques (the AIM/model-statement query returned only adjacent Vrij cognitive-load material). Confidence: low / unresolved. Open question below.

## Q2 — Méndez Principles (2021) and HIG research

The Méndez Principles on Effective Interviewing for Investigations and Information-Gathering (May 2021) were coordinated by the Association for the Prevention of Torture, the Anti-Torture Initiative (American University), and the Norwegian Centre for Human Rights. They codify science- and rights-based interviewing: rapport-building, information-gathering (not confession-seeking), and non-coercive method as both more humane and more effective. They explicitly build on research from the US High-Value Detainee Interrogation Group (HIG, est. 2010 post-torture-program fallout), which funded a substantial empirical program (FBI/CIA/DoD researchers) on lawful, non-coercive interrogation effectiveness. Confidence: high — multiple independent sources (Wikipedia, COST network, Just Security, Penn CERL, APT) converge on the same history and content. Sources: [Méndez Principles — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A9ndez_Principles_on_Effective_Interviewing); [The science behind effective interviewing for investigations](https://www.cost.eu/effective-interviewing-for-investigations-implemendez/); [Effective investigative interviewing without torture](https://www.justsecurity.org/146367/effective-investigative-interviewing-without-torture/); [Mendez Principles — five years on](https://www.apt.ch/news/interrogation-effective-interviewing-five-years-mendez-principles) (2026, i.e., recent/current coverage, good recency per the 12-month-freshness rule). Contrast: the **Reid Technique** is accusatorial — presumes guilt before the interrogation phase begins, uses psychological pressure/manipulation, and is explicitly single-mindedly confession-seeking rather than information-seeking. Multiple 2024-2026 sources (including a 2025 Ontario Court of Appeal case, *R v Ordonio*, where defense counsel argued Reid-induced statements should be presumptively inadmissible) describe mounting legal and scientific backlash: interrogators using Reid-style methods are not reliably better than chance at distinguishing true from false denials, and Reid is described as risking false confessions especially in juveniles, people with intellectual disabilities, and people with mental health conditions, because the technique "can break down the innocent as well as the guilty." Confidence: high on the criticism's substance (repeated across independent legal/academic/news sources, recent 2024-2026 dates); the overall contrast is one of the best-supported dichotomies in this research pass. Sources: [The Reid Technique (Penn State, 2024)](https://sites.psu.edu/aspsy/2024/02/28/the-reid-technique); [Famed police interrogation technique led to false confessions (Nebraska coverage, July 2026)](https://www.1011now.com/2026/07/09/famed-police-interrogation-technique-led-infamous-false-confessions-nebraska-we-still-use-it/); [The cutting edge of confession evidence (Texas Law Review)](https://texaslawreview.org/the-cutting-edge-of-confession-evidence-redefining-coercion-and-reforming-police-interrogation-techniques-in-the-american-criminal-justice-system/). Mapping: directly supports PRB-3/PRB-4/AST-10 — the arena's entire asymmetric-scoring design (false-positive gate before recall ranking) is aligned with the Méndez/HIG evidence base that confidence in an accusation must be earned by content, not presumed from demeanor or produced by pressure; it also argues the coach's "neutral follow-up" constraint (never leading, never accusatory) is the information-gathering model, not Reid's confession-first model.

## Q3 — Demeanor and deception

**Bond & DePaulo (2006)** meta-analyzed 206 documents / 24,483 judges: average deception-detection accuracy across all studies = ~54% (vs. 50% chance), with truths correctly classified ~61% of the time and lies only ~47% — i.e., human judges have a "truth bias" and are barely above chance even when motivated and trained. Confidence: high — this is among the most-cited, most-replicated figures in the field, confirmed by the ACLU-hosted primary PDF and PubMed abstract. Sources: [Accuracy of deception judgments — PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16859438/); [primary PDF via ACLU FOIA release](https://assets.aclu.org/live/uploads/document/foia/2006-Personality-and-Social-Psychology-Review-Accuracy-of-Deception-Judgements.pdf).

**DePaulo et al. (2003)**, Psychological Bulletin, synthesized 1,338 estimates across 158 candidate behavioral cues (nonverbal + verbal): liars are on average less forthcoming, tell less compelling/detailed stories, make a more negative impression, and seem more tense — but the median effect size across all cues was only d ≈ 0.10 (very small), and many commonly-assumed cues (eye contact, fidgeting, etc.) showed no reliable link to deception at all. Effects were stronger when the lie was about a real transgression and the liar was highly motivated by identity-relevant stakes. Confidence: high — landmark, frequently re-cited, PDF of the original paper retrieved. Source: [DePaulo et al., Cues to Deception (full PDF, MIT Media Lab mirror)](https://smg.media.mit.edu/library/DePauloEtAl.Cues%20to%20Deception.pdf); [PubMed abstract](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12555795/).

**Stress/confusion in truthful people** is the flip side of the same literature: because cues like tension, hesitation, and non-fluency are *not* reliable deception markers (DePaulo's near-zero effect sizes), a truthful-but-stressed or truthful-but-uncertain subject will produce the same surface signals as a nervous liar — this is the empirical backbone for PRB-4 ("nervousness, demeanor... must never be shortcuts to a deception label"). Confidence: high, as a direct logical/empirical consequence of DePaulo (2003) and Bond & DePaulo (2006) — not a separate citation but the same evidence base read for its negative claim.

**Accent and credibility bias — Lev-Ari & Keysar (2010),** Journal of Experimental Social Psychology: American listeners rated trivia statements read by native speakers as more truthful (7.5/9) than statements read by speakers with a mild (6.95) or heavy (6.84) foreign accent, even though participants were explicitly told the statements were scripted and not sourced from the speaker's own knowledge. Mechanism: listeners misattribute the processing difficulty of accented speech (reduced "fluency") to the truthfulness of the content, not to the speaker. Confidence: high — original researcher, journal, and mechanism are consistently reported across ScienceDaily, BPS Research Digest, and academic mirrors. Sources: [ScienceDaily coverage](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2010/07/100719164002.htm); [BPS Research Digest](https://bps.org.uk/research-digest/speakers-foreign-accent-are-perceived-less-credible). Mapping: this is the primary citation grounding SCN-3 (vary communication style independently of role) and the PRB-4 audit requirement — a credibility penalty purely from accent/fluency is a measurable, well-replicated human bias; the arena's bake-off should explicitly test whether assistant candidates reproduce it (flag rate conditioned on simulated accent/non-fluency markers in subject text, holding role constant).

## Q4 — Question typology

Standard typology used in interview-training/coding literature: **open/invitational (TED: Tell/Explain/Describe)**, **probing (5WH: who/what/when/where/why/how)**, **closed (yes/no or single-fact)**, **leading** (presupposes/suggests the answer), **suggestive**, **compound** (multiple questions bundled), **forced-choice**, **opinion/option-posing**. NICHD-protocol research (used mainly in child forensic interviewing, but its question-effect findings generalize to adult investigative interviewing pedagogy) repeatedly shows: training interviewers on structured open-question use measurably increases open-question rate and the forensic relevance/detail of answers, and reduces suggestive/leading question use; "no other technique has been proven to be similarly effective" per one synthesis. Confidence: high on the open > closed > leading effectiveness ordering (extremely well replicated); medium on exact magnitude claims (varies by study/sample). Source: [A Structured Interview Protocol Improves the Quality and Informativeness of Investigative Interviews (National Children's Advocacy Center PDF)](https://www.nationalcac.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/A-Structured-Interview-protocol-Improves-the-quality-and-informativeness-of-investigative-interviews.pdf). Mapping: directly actionable for EVL-7 dimension 1 ("clarity and neutrality") and the AST-6 per-question grading — the coach/rubric can operationalize question type as a closed enum (open/probing/closed/leading/suggestive/compound/forced-choice/opinion) and score neutrality mechanically off that enum before any semantic judgment, which is cheap, auditable, and well precedented.

## Q5 — Evasion vs. uncertainty vs. legitimate non-disclosure vs. poorly-framed question (EVL-8)

**Equivocation theory (Bavelas et al., 1990):** equivocation ("non-straightforward... ambiguous, contradictory, tangential, obscure, evasive") arises from a "communicative avoidance-avoidance conflict" — a question where every direct answer carries some cost, yet a reply is still socially expected. This gives a principled *reason* a truthful, non-deceptive subject might equivocate (reputational/legal/social risk) distinct from concealing a violation. **Bull's typology** (with colleagues) catalogued **43 distinct techniques for not directly answering a question**, developed originally for coding political-interview evasion, and argues responses form a continuum from full reply through "intermediate responses" to complete non-reply, rather than a reply/non-reply binary. Confidence: medium — concept and 43-technique count both independently corroborated across academic sources (SAGE encyclopedia entry, peer-reviewed journal abstracts), though full primary coding scheme text wasn't retrieved this pass. Sources: [Equivocation — SAGE Encyclopedia of Human Relationships](https://sk.sagepub.com/ency/edvol/embed/humanrelationships/chpt/equivocation); [The analysis of political equivocation by British political leaders](https://budrich-journals.de/index.php/pcs/article/view/45859). **Clayman's conversation-analytic work on evasion** was referenced in training materials found (political-interview CA coding) but no primary Clayman citation was independently retrieved this pass — treat as an open item (see below). Mapping: this is the core literature for building EVL-8's annotator guideline. Recommended working taxonomy derived from the sources: (1) **evasion** = an avoidance-avoidance response where the subject has disclosable information relevant to the question and withholds/deflects it beyond what the profile's permitted-behavior list allows (SUB-6); (2) **genuine uncertainty** = subject lacks the knowledge (SUB-2's "may be uncertain; say when they do not know") — content-marked by explicit epistemic hedging tied to a plausible gap, not topic-avoidance; (3) **legitimate non-disclosure** = subject's profile permits withholding this specific fact (privacy/role-appropriate boundary) — requires checking against the private subject packet's disclosure policy (SCN-8), which the coach/scorer has access to but the investigator does not; (4) **poorly framed question** = the non-answer is attributable to compound/ambiguous/double-barreled phrasing on the investigator's side, not the subject's choice — this is the one category that should suppress an evasion flag and instead feed back to the investigator's own rubric score (EVL-7 dimension 1, clarity).

## Q6 — Efficacy of simulated/avatar interview training (bearing on KPI-1's +20%)

**Pompedda et al.** avatar-training studies (child protective-services workers and novice students interviewing computer-generated child avatars) found training-with-feedback **measurably improved interview quality in the short term, with no substantial decline after 4 months**; feedback was split into *outcome feedback* (conclusions about what happened) and *process feedback* (appropriateness of question types used). Prior experience did not predict quality and did not moderate the training effect — avatar training helped novices and experienced workers alike. Effects were shown to transfer at least partially to interviews with real children in mock-event studies. Confidence: medium — multiple independent Frontiers/University of Turku sources converge on direction and durability, but no single study in this pass reported a clean percentage-improvement figure directly comparable to KPI-1's "+20% questioning score." Sources: [Experience and Long-Term Training Effects in Simulated Child Sexual Abuse Interviews (Frontiers)](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.753111/full); [University of Turku publication record](https://research.utu.fi/converis/portal/detail/Publication/491736562?lang=en_GB). Judgment call (not a recommendation, just an inference for the build): a +20% questioning-score gain from targeted process feedback (naming question type, flagging leading/closed questions, suggesting the specific open/probing alternative) is in the same *direction and rough magnitude* as what the avatar-training literature reports for short-term skill gains, which argues KPI-1 is plausible for a single-session practice-to-post-test design *if* the feedback is specific and tied to the five rubric dimensions (process feedback), not just an outcome verdict. It does NOT by itself establish that a single hackathon-scale volunteer study (per BRIEF ambiguity #6) will reach significance — sample size and baseline variance remain open questions.

## Q7 — Behavioral anchors for 0-4 scoring of the five rubric dimensions (EVL-7)

Direct search for a pre-built, publicly documented 0-4 behaviorally-anchored investigative-interview rubric returned nothing usable — results were dominated by unrelated hiring/behavioral-interview-question content (tldv.io blog spam) with zero relevant hits. Confidence: low / **gap confirmed, not filled**. This is a genuine open question, not a weak-confidence finding — treat the rubric anchors as something the team must author internally. What the other questions *do* supply as raw material for authoring anchors: (a) the open/probing/closed/leading/suggestive/compound/forced-choice/opinion question-type enum (Q4) can mechanically anchor "clarity and neutrality" (0 = leading/suggestive/compound; 4 = clean open or targeted probing with no presupposition); (b) Vrij's unanticipated-question / cognitive-load criteria (Q1) can anchor "evidence-based follow-up" and "testing alternative explanations" (does the follow-up ask for an unanticipated, checkable, spatial/temporal detail tied to disclosed evidence, vs. a generic or closed probe); (c) SUE's statement-evidence-inconsistency logic (Q1) can anchor "testing alternative explanations" directly (did the investigator return to the evidence already released to test the subject's account against it); (d) the EVL-8 evasion taxonomy (Q5) supplies the discriminators needed for "response relevance" scoring (did the investigator recognize a non-responsive answer as such and press, vs. accept it); (e) EX-3 ("insufficient evidence... verify the work order") is the deck's own worked example of "supported closure" at a high anchor level. None of this is a substitute for a validated rubric — it is scaffolding the team would need to draft and pilot-calibrate per EVL-7's own instruction ("Trainers must calibrate it before use").

## Q8 — Workplace/administrative/federal investigative interviewing guidance

OIG-style administrative investigations (reviewed via Green Book Standards references) distinguish **witness vs. subject** notice obligations, typically occur under oath/recorded, and explicitly withhold allegation specifics until the actual interview (to protect investigation integrity) while still advising the interviewee of their status and the pertinent allegations at the interview itself. Security-clearance **background-investigation subject interviews** (SF-86 verification) are explicitly framed as credibility-assessment interviews bound to a prior written disclosure (the SF-86), which is structurally close to the arena's locked-case-facts model (SCN-1/SCN-4). Administrative-investigation interviewer style is commonly taxonomized into **Factual** (objective, evidence-sequenced), **Emotional** (empathetic, motivation-focused), and **Thematic/Hybrid** — note this source frames the *goal* as "encouraging truthful admissions," which is closer to the accusatorial/Reid family than to Méndez/HIG information-gathering, and should be read with that bias in mind rather than adopted uncritically. Confidence: medium — sources are practitioner/compliance-vendor pages (CaseIQ, FedSmith, municipal OIG FAQs) rather than peer-reviewed research; useful for procedural framing (notice, recording, oath) but not for behavioral-science grounding. Sources: [Interviewing Investigation Subjects: Best Practices (CaseIQ)](https://caseiq.com/resources/interviewing-investigation-subjects-best-practices); [Guidelines for Conducting Investigative Interviews (FedSmith, 2021)](https://www.fedsmith.com/2021/10/18/guidelines-conducting-investigative-interviews/); [OIG — What to Expect When Contacted](https://www.cabq.gov/inspectorgeneral/oig-frequently-asked-questions-faq/what-to-expect-when-contacted-by-a-member-of-the-oig-investagative-staff). Mapping: directly supports the slide-8 synthetic-case framing (EX-1..EX-4): "Why did you enter?"/"It was a busy shift" plus "verify the work order and timeline" (EX-3) is squarely in the administrative-investigation register (routine workplace access-control question), not a criminal-interrogation one — reinforcing that the arena's register should stay Factual/evidence-sequenced (Méndez-aligned) rather than Thematic/admission-seeking (Reid-aligned).

## Contradictions and disputed points

1. **CBCA/RM accuracy claims vs. general distrust of content-analysis tools in court.** Sources say CBCA/RM are "above chance" and used in actual criminal proceedings in some jurisdictions, yet the same literature flags weak ecological validity in the lab paradigms that produced those accuracy numbers. Treat any single accuracy percentage for CBCA/RM as contested rather than settled.
2. **Reid-style Thematic/admission-seeking technique still appears in current (2026) workplace-investigation guidance** (CaseIQ's three-style taxonomy) even as peer-reviewed/legal literature (Q2) is moving hard against Reid-family accusatorial methods and toward Méndez/HIG. The field is not unified; current practitioner guidance lags the research consensus.
3. **Vrij's cognitive-load/unanticipated-question numbers (71%/56%) vs. Bond & DePaulo's near-chance baseline (54%).** These are not strictly contradictory (different methodologies — Vrij's are *structured interview techniques* judged against transcripts/outcomes with ground truth, Bond & DePaulo is *naive human judgment accuracy* across hundreds of studies) but a team using Vrij's more optimistic figures should not imply they generalize to untrained/ad hoc judgment, which the Bond & DePaulo baseline represents.
4. **SUE's 85.4%/56.1% figures** were found only in a secondary citation (CaseIQ blog), not independently cross-verified against a Granhag/Hartwig primary paper this pass — flag as needing a primary-source check before being quoted as a KPI anchor.

## Open questions

1. Primary-source verification still needed for: SUE's 85.4%/56.1% detection-accuracy figures; a current (2020s) CBCA/RM/Verifiability-Approach accuracy meta-analysis with a single comparable percentage; Clayman's specific conversation-analytic evasion-coding scheme; "Asymmetric Information Management" and "Model Statement" technique (no primary source retrieved this pass at all — may need a differently-worded query or may not be the field's standard term; could be conflated with a different author's naming).
2. No publicly documented 0-4 behaviorally-anchored investigative-interview rubric was found — EVL-7's anchors will need to be authored and piloted in-house (Q7).
3. Whether a hackathon-scale volunteer study (BRIEF ambiguity #6) can produce a statistically defensible KPI-1 (+20%) figure given likely small N and the between-subject variance the avatar-training literature doesn't resolve for a single short session.
4. Whether EVL-8's "legitimate non-disclosure" category needs its own explicit tag in the private subject packet (SCN-8) so the fidelity judge/scorer can distinguish it from evasion without seeing the evaluator-only packet (SCN-9) — this is an annotator-guideline design decision, not just a literature gap.

## Implications for the arena build

- The SUE mechanic (withhold → disclose late/strategically → test for statement-evidence inconsistency) is close to a 1:1 match for SCN-4/SCN-10's scripted evidence release and AST-3's "neutral follow-up using the evidence" — this is the strongest, most directly implementable piece of science in this route; consider citing it explicitly in the system prompt design for the coaching assistant.
- Vrij's unanticipated-question / cognitive-load technique is the single cheapest, most prompt-engineerable lever for a text-only coach (ask for sequence/spatial/temporal detail tied to the evidence just released) and should be a named strategy the assistant can choose, not just "ask a follow-up."
- DePaulo (2003) and Bond & DePaulo (2006), plus Lev-Ari & Keysar (2010), are the direct evidentiary basis for PRB-4's hard rule (style/demeanor/accent are not deception evidence) — strong enough to justify a style-stratified false-positive audit as described in PRB-4's implication column, and strong enough to justify explicitly penalizing (in scoring or training data) any assistant candidate whose flags correlate with subject-style markers rather than content.
- The open/probing/closed/leading/suggestive/compound/forced-choice/opinion question-type enum (Q4) is reusable as a cheap, auditable first-pass signal for both AST-6 (grading the investigator's question) and EVL-7 dimension 1 (clarity and neutrality) — classify question type mechanically, then layer semantic judgment on top.
- The Méndez/HIG vs. Reid contrast (Q2) gives a defensible, citable reason the whole system is built as information-gathering/non-accusatorial rather than confession-seeking — useful for the written justification of why the coach is barred from suggesting leading or accusatory follow-ups, and for framing the EX-4 ground rule ("evasive wording alone does not prove a violation").
- EVL-8's annotator guideline should formalize four categories (evasion / genuine uncertainty / legitimate non-disclosure / poorly-framed question) per Q5's synthesis — Bavelas's avoidance-avoidance-conflict framing is a good one-sentence definition of "evasion" for the annotator instructions, and the fourth category (poorly framed question) should route to the investigator's own clarity score rather than to a subject-evasion flag.
- KPI-1 (+20%) is directionally supported by feedback-based simulated-interview training literature (Pompedda) but not numerically validated by any single source found — flag to the team that the number should be treated as an aspirational target whose statistical defensibility depends on sample size design, not an evidence-backed guarantee.
- Several sub-claims (SUE's specific percentages, a validated 0-4 rubric, AIM/model-statement) remain unverified at primary-source level; before hard-coding any of these numbers into product copy, scoring code, or the pitch deck, verify against the primary paper.
